body.p: To trace the establishment of God’s plan to overcome sin through his chosen people, Yisrael (Israel)
Records primeval events and events from the patriarchal period (ca. 2100–1700 BC)
A variety of places in the Middle East, focusing heavily on the patriarchs during their time in Kena’an (Canaan) and Mitsrayim (Egypt)
To recount the deliverance of the Hebrews from Mitsrayim (Egypt) and the establishment of their covenant and worship practices
Records events that likely occurred in either 1526–1446 BC or 1350–1270 BC
Begins with the Hebrews in slavery in Mitsrayim and ends with the covenant people of God en route to the Promised Land
To demonstrate God’s holiness and point his people to lead holy lives
Records events that likely occurred around either 1446 BC or 1270 BC
The Israelis (Israelites) had been established as God’s covenant people and were camped at the foot of Mount Sinay (Sinai)
To document the transition from the unfaithful generation who left Mitsrayim (Egypt) to the generation who would enter the Promised Land
Records events that likely occurred around either 1445–1406 BC or 1269–1230 BC
The book begins with the Israelis (Israelites) at Sinay (Sinai), traces their journey through the wilderness, and closes with them in the plains of Moav (Moab) at the doorstep of the Promised Land
To reiterate and expand on the covenant prior to Mosheh’s (Moses’) death and the people’s entry into the Promised Land
The Israelis (Israelites) are on the verge of entering the Promised Land, and Mosheh is nearing the end of his life
To recount Yisrael’s (Israel’s) conquest of the Promised Land
Records events that likely occurred in either 1406–1376 BC or 1230–1200 BC
Begins with the Israelis (Israelites) about to cross the Yarden (Jordan) and ends with their new land having been distributed
To describe the period of the judges and to present a case for an Israeli (Israelite) monarchy
Records events that occurred in either 1376–1050 BC or 1200–1050 BC
Yisrael (Israel) was failing to fully conquer the Promised Land and faced repeated oppression from enemies
To tell the inspiring story of Ruth and to trace the background of King David
Records events that occurred around 1100 BC
The period of the judges, during and immediately after a famine that had struck Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem)
To recount the establishment of the Israeli (Israelite) monarchy and to highlight the differing character of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) first two kings
Records events that occurred around 1050–1011 BC
The transition from the period of the judges to the Israeli monarchy
To describe the reign of David and to demonstrate God’s commitment to David’s line
Records events that occurred around 1011–971 BC
Following Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) death, David sought to establish his throne over all Yisrael (Israel) and to expand Israeli (Israelite) territory
To outline the glory of Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) reign, the division of the kingdom, and the degradation of Yisrael (Israel)
Records events that occurred around 973–853 BC
Begins at the high point of the Israeli (Israelite) monarchy (Shelomoh’s reign) and ends with a divided kingdom and a low point in the Israeli monarchy (Ahav’s (Ahab’s) reign)
To clarify why both Yisrael (Israel) and Yehudah (Judah) were experiencing exile from the Promised Land
Records events that occurred around 853–586 BC
Continues the story from 1 Kings of the divided kingdom, ending with both kingdoms experiencing exile
To instill hope—largely by appeal to the Davidic promise—among Yehudim (Jews) who had returned to their land but were living in subjugation
Likely written around 400 BC, largely recording events that occurred around 1011–971 BC
Judea had been resettled by Yehudim following the Exile, but these Yehudim were still living under foreign (Persian) rule; the account essentially traces the reign of David
To give readers hope for a restored kingdom of Yisrael (Israel) characterized by proper worship
Likely written around 400 BC, recording events that occurred around 971–538 BC
Postexilic Judea during Persian rule; the account begins with the reign of Shelomoh (Solomon) and ends with Koresh’s (Cyrus’) proclamation allowing the people to return to Judea
To demonstrate God’s continued provision for his people and to show how to live when faced with foreign control, opposition, and pagan influence
Records events that occurred around 538–457 BC
Yerushalem (Jerusalem), beginning with the initial return of Yehudim (Jews) from exile and ending with Ezra’s arrival there
To recount the reconstruction of Yerushalem’s (Jerusalem’s) walls and to demonstrate God’s faithfulness to those dedicated to him
Records events that occurred around 445–430 BC
Yerushalem, approximately fifteen years after Ezra had arrived
To demonstrate God’s providential care of his people and to trace the origin of the Festivalfeast of Purim
Records events that occurred around 483–473 BC
The Persian capital, Shushan (Susa), during the reign of Ahashverosh (Xerxes), after a number of Yehudim (Jews) had returned to Judea
To offer reflection on the issue of human suffering, primarily by questioning the oft-held connection between moral goodness and prosperity
The patriarchal period, possibly in the land of Edom
To offer praise and prayer to God, to supply God’s people with texts for worship, and to provide reflection on the sovereignty of God and some of life’s toughest questions
Various; nearly half are linked with David
Written over the course of many centuries; the process of collecting and editing was likely completed after the Babylonian exile
Varied, but a postexilic setting accounts for much of the editorial activity and grouping of the psalms
To offer practical wisdom for making decisions and ordering life
Various; many are attributed to Shelomoh (Solomon)
Written and compiled over the course of several centuries, beginning during Shelomoh’s reign (971–931 BC) and continuing until at least the reign of Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) (728–686 BC)
Part is directed to a young man; other parts hint at diverse settings
To reflect on the meaning and enjoyment of life
The overwhelmingly prosperous—but apparently unsatisfying—reign of King Shelomoh
The Book of Song of Songs
To celebrate God’s gifts of love and sexuality
The book is associated with Shelomoh’s reign, but its lack of clear plotline discredits any strong identification of setting
To warn Yehudah (Judah) of impending judgment and to offer hope concerning a remnant of God’s people
The southern kingdom of Yehudah, around the time of Ashur’s (Assyria’s) conquest of the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel)
To warn Yehudah (Judah) of coming destruction, outline the reasons for God’s judgment, and encourage renewed devotion to the Lord
Content stems from Yirmiyah; possibly written down by Baruk (Baruch)
The final years of the kingdom of Yehudah, the invasion and destruction of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) by the Babylonians, and the initial years of Yehudah’s exile
To express deep sorrow over the destruction of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and to offer a glimmer of hope to God’s people
The aftermath of the Babylonian invasion, the destruction of Yerushalem, and the exile of the people of Yehudah (Judah)
To pronounce the impending judgment on Yehudah (Judah) and to offer hope following Yerushalem’s (Jerusalem’s) destruction
Exile in Bavel (Babylon), immediately before, during, and after the destruction of Yerushalem
To demonstrate God’s sovereignty over all, including powers apathetic or antagonistic toward him
Bavel (Babylon), beginning with the first wave of exiles from Yehudah (Judah) and ending around the time of Koresh’s (Cyrus’) decree allowing Yehudim (Jews) to return home
To depict Yisrael’s (Israel’s) unfaithfulness and ensuing judgment, and to show God’s desire to heal and restore his people
The northern kingdom of Yisrael, in the days leading up to its destruction at the hands of Ashur (Assyria)
To display God’s sovereignty and judgment, to spur readers to repentance, and to promise restoration
The land of Yehudah (Judah), during a catastrophic locust plague (interpreted variously as literal or figurative)
To confront the northern kingdom’s apostasy and oppression of the marginalized
The shrine at Beyt-El (Bethel) in the northern kingdom, during the reign of Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II
To announce God’s judgment on Edom, who had rejoiced at and participated in Yehudah’s (Judah’s) destruction
Probably very soon after the destruction of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) by the Babylonians
To recount a story of the far-reaching scope of God’s sovereignty and salvation
A time when Ashur’s (Assyria’s) influence in Yisrael (Israel) had temporarily decreased, likely during the reign of Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II
To proclaim judgment against Shomron (Samaria) and Yerushalem (Jerusalem), but also to offer a strong message of hope for Yisrael’s (Israel’s) future
The northern kingdom of Yisrael shortly before its destruction and the southern kingdom of Yehudah (Judah) during the reigns of Yotam (Jotham), Ahaz, and Hizkiyah (Hezekiah)
To announce God’s coming judgment on Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, thus offering hope to the people of Yehudah (Judah)
The Assyrian Empire had conquered the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel), and now the southern kingdom of Yehudah was in danger of facing the same fate
To address some difficult questions about God’s purposes and the presence of evil in the world
The final years of the independent kingdom of Yehudah (Judah), when Assyrian power was weakening but Babylonian power was increasing
To warn of the coming “day of Yahweh” and to urge repentance
Near the beginning of King Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) reign in Yehudah (Judah), before his religious reforms
To encourage the Yehudim (Jews) to resume Temple reconstruction and to promote spiritual renewal
Yerushalem (Jerusalem), almost twenty years after Koresh (Cyrus) had allowed the Yehudim to return and rebuild the Temple
To foster spiritual renewal and to announce a grand future for the people of God
Yerushalem (Jerusalem), a couple of decades after a remnant of Yehudim (Jews) had returned from exile
To reorient the people to proper conduct in relationships and worship
Postexilic Judea, during Persian control, after the Temple had been rebuilt
The Gospel of Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios)
To demonstrate that Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) is the Messiah and to help Christians understand how to live in relation to Youdaismos (Judaism)
Matay (also known as Levi), one of the twelve apostles of Yeshua
Written at a time in which early Christians were struggling to make sense of the relationship of their new beliefs to the Jewish faith
To relay the Good News about Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), who is the Messiah and Son of God
Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos, who according to early tradition put in writing the recollections of the apostle Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros)
Likely written sometime during the late 60s AD

Written at a time in which Christians in the Roman world were facing persecution—necessitating that the gospel traditions begin to be written down—and Yerushalem’s (Jerusalem’s) destruction was imminent
To write a reliable historical account of the life of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) that would confirm the truth of the Christian message
Lukas, a physician and occasional companion of the apostle Paulos (Paul)
Either around AD 59–63, during Paulos’s imprisonment in Romai (Rome), or between AD 70–90, using the Gospel of Markos (Mark) as a source

Written during a time of increasing tension between Yehudim (Jews) and Christians, in which Lukas sought to demonstrate that those—both Yehudi (Jew) and Gentile—who believed that Yeshua was the Messiah made up the new people of God
The Gospel of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes)
To generate belief in Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) as Messiah and Son of God and to connect this belief with eternal life
Likely the “beloved disciple,” traditionally identified as Yohan, son of Zavday (Zebedee)
Written toward the end of Yohan’s life during a time when the early followers of Yeshua were facing strife from local meeting halls
To describe the spread of the Good News of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ and the birth of the church from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) throughout the Roman world
Lukas (Luke), a physician and occasional companion of the apostle Paulos (Paul)

Likely between the early 60s AD and the mid-80s AD. The events recorded in Acts end in the early 60s, but a commonly held view suggests that it was written later, presuming that Lukas’s Gospel used the Gospel of Markos (Mark)—likely written in the late 60s—as a source
Written during a time when the Good News of Yeshua had spread throughout the Mediterranean world and it had become evident that God’s salvation extended to both Yehudim (Jews) and Gentiles
To outline the Good News and to address the theological and social divisions that had arisen in a church comprised of both Yehudim (Jews) and Gentiles
Likely around AD 57, near the end of his third missionary journey

Written—probably in Korinthos (Corinth)—toward the end of Paulos’s missionary activity, when he was making plans to visit the church in Romai (Rome) on his way to Spania (Spain), after delivering a gift to the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) church
Paulos’s (Paul’s) First Letter to the Corinthians
To clarify some questions the Korinthios (Corinthian) church had raised and to address a series of specific problems that had arisen in the church there

Written from Efesos (Ephesus) during Paulos’s third missionary journey, in response to reports and questions he had received from the church in Korinthos (Corinth) (see 1 Cor 1:11; 5:1; 7:1; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1)
Paulos’s (Paul’s) Second Letter to the Corinthians
To defend Paulos’s apostolic authority and to squelch the influence of false teachers

Written after Paulos received a positive report from Titos (Titus) about the Korinthios (Corinthian) church’s repentance, which had followed from a previous letter (now lost) that Paulos had sent to them (see 2 Cor 7:5-9)

To persuade the Gentile Christians in Galatia—against opposition from certain Jewish Christians—that it is unnecessary to be circumcised and to adopt other practices from Jewish law in order to be part of God’s people
Likely AD 48 or 49, just prior to the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) council
Written after a group of Jewish Christians had infiltrated the Galatikos (Galatian) church communities, teaching on the necessity of practicing circumcision
To outline the scope of God’s grace, encourage unity among Jewish and Gentile believers, and demonstrate what new life in Christ looks like
Traditionally, AD 60–62, but possibly earlier, around AD 53–56

Written while Paulos was in prison, probably either in Romai (Rome) or Efesos (Ephesus), after the Good News had spread throughout Asia Minor and the believers in that region needed further instruction regarding the implications of their new faith
To thank the Philippians for their recent gift and to encourage them to experience joy and contentment in the midst of their suffering
Traditionally, AD 60–62, but possibly earlier, around AD 53–56
Written while Paulos was in prison and while the church at Filippou (Philippi)—which had recently sent Paulos a financial gift—was also undergoing persecution
To combat false teaching at Kolossai (Colosse) by emphasizing the supremacy of Christ and by insisting that true spiritual growth and ethical living stem from him
Traditionally, AD 60–62, but possibly earlier, around AD 53–56
Written while Paulos was in prison, after he had heard—presumably from Epafras (Epaphras)—about the false teaching that had arisen in the church at Kolossai
Paulos’s (Paul’s) First Letter to the Thessalonians
To express thanksgiving for the faith of the Thessalonikai (Thessalonian) believers and to give them further instruction about Christian behavior and the Lord’s return
Written while Paulos was in Korinthos (Corinth), after he had received a positive report from Timotheos about the church in Thessalonikai
Paulos’s (Paul’s) Second Letter to the Thessalonians
To instill hope in the midst of persecution and to address false teaching and idleness in the community
Written soon after 1 Thessalonians, after persecution had increased in Thessalonikai (Thessalonica) and false teaching had emerged
To provide guidance to Timotheos for addressing false teaching and instructing the church on proper conduct
Written near the end of Paulos’s life, after Paulos had sent Timotheos to Efesos (Ephesus) to halt false teaching in the church
To commission Timotheos to continue the work Paulos had begun and to encourage Timotheos to endure suffering
Probably written during Paulos’s second imprisonment in Romai (Rome), shortly before his death—which he understood to be imminent
To give Titos instruction on the establishment of church leaders on Kraitai (Crete) and to promote proper conduct among the believers there
Written near the end of Paulos’s life, while Titos was on the island of Kraitai, a place known for its degenerate culture
To encourage Filemon to welcome back his slave Onesimos (Onesimus), who had become a believer
Traditionally, AD 60–62, but possibly earlier, around AD 53–56
Written while Paulos was in prison, after he had encountered Onesimos, who was seemingly a runaway slave of Filemon, a Christian leader in Kolossai (Colosse)
To encourage perseverance in the face of suffering, primarily by highlighting the superiority of Christ and the sufficiency of his work
Most likely the early 60s AD, but a date after AD 70 is also possible
Written to a group of Christians—likely in Romai (Rome)—who were facing persecution and struggling to maintain their faith
To share practical wisdom and to challenge readers to maintain their faith—a faith that is active and other-focused
Ya’akov, brother of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus)
Written—presumably from Yerushalem (Jerusalem)—to Jewish believers who had scattered following the persecution which began with the martyrdom of Stefanos (Stephen)
The First Letter of Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros)
To encourage believers who were suffering to maintain a life of holiness and thereby bear witness to Christ
Written toward the end of Kefa’s life to believers in northern Asia Minor who were experiencing persecution
The Second Letter of Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros)
To denounce false teachers and to encourage continued growth in the faith
Written to the same groups of believers addressed in 1 Kefa, whose communities were being infiltrated by false teachers
The First Letter of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes)
To affirm correct belief concerning Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ, to exhort believers to love one another, and to provide assurance about eternal life
Written to a community that had recently experienced a schism due to the emergence of a heretical faction
The Second Letter of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes)
To outline the appropriate response to false teachers and to encourage believers to love one another
Written to a community of believers—probably in Asia Minor—who had either already encountered false teachers or were likely to do so soon
The Third Letter of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes)
To commend Gaios (Gaius) for his hospitality to the apostle’s emissaries and to reprove Diotrefes (Diotrephes)
Written to an individual named Gaios, in response to his hospitality and to the lack thereof by a man named Diotrefes
The Letter of Yehudah (Jude; Grk. Yudas)
To urge readers to defend their faith in the face of false teaching
Yehudah, brother of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus)
Unknown, possibly around the same time as 2 Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) (early 60s AD)
Written to a group of churches that had been infiltrated by false teachers who encouraged an immoral lifestyle
To challenge readers to remain faithful in the midst of persecution by pointing them to God’s victory over evil and to their future hope
Most likely the AD 90s, but possibly the AD 60s
Written to a group of churches in Asia who were experiencing persecution at the hands of the Roman Empire
